title: Magma underground, lava on the surface: one rock, two names
description: Molten rock has two names, and the difference is simply address. Underground it is magma; the moment it erupts onto the surface, scientists call the very same material lava.

body.heading: Where magma waits
paragraphs: Deep beneath a volcano, melted rock collects in a magma chamber. It is not pure liquid like water — it is a thick, slow mixture of molten rock, crystals and trapped gases, hotter than 700 degrees Celsius.
Those trapped gases matter. Like the fizz in a shaken bottle, they build pressure as magma rises, which is why some eruptions ooze gently and others explode.

body.heading: The moment it becomes lava
paragraphs: When molten rock breaks through the surface — from a crater, a crack or a side vent — its name changes to lava. Nothing about the rock itself changes at that instant; only its location does.
As lava flows and cools it hardens into new rock, building cones, islands and whole landscapes. Given enough eruptions over enough time, lava does not just cover the land — it becomes the land.

takeaway: Magma is molten rock underground; lava is the same molten rock after it erupts onto the surface.
